speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext: On the orders of the day:

speakeroldname: Right Hon. J. G. Diefenbaker (Leader of the Opposition):
speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: NORTH AMERICAN GENERAL INSURANCE COMPANY-INVESTIGATION RESPECTING COLLAPSE OF COMPANY AND PARTICIPATION IN FRAUDULENT PRACTICES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as this matter covers several departments I should like to direct my question to the Prime Minister. It has to do with the North American General Insurance Company, which is a federally incorporated company, a subsidiary of Prudential Finance, and other companies today causing tremendous losses to Canadian workers, pensioners and investors, and a loss of faith in financial institutions.
I should like to ask the Prime Minister what investigation has been undertaken by the Department of Insurance into the circumstances surrounding the collapse of the North American General Insurance Company. I should also like to ask whether there is any truth in the statement, apparently well supported by documentary evidence, to the effect
Inquiries of the Ministry that in January, 1966, William Gruber made allegations of fraud and misappropriation to officers of the Department of Insurance, the Department of National Revenue and the bankruptcy division in respect of Prudential Finance, one of the associated companies.
What action does the government intend to take so that people, who have suffered grievously as a result of financial manoeuvring and manipulation, will have some hope that their savings will not be lost to them, especially since they relied on the fact that this is a dominion company?

speakeroldname: Righi Hon. L. B. Pearson (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister
subtopic: NORTH AMERICAN GENERAL INSURANCE COMPANY-INVESTIGATION RESPECTING COLLAPSE OF COMPANY AND PARTICIPATION IN FRAUDULENT PRACTICES
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I have discussed this matter with the Minister of Finance who has been investigating it. I am going to ask him to reply to the questions.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: NORTH AMERICAN GENERAL INSURANCE COMPANY-INVESTIGATION RESPECTING COLLAPSE OF COMPANY AND PARTICIPATION IN FRAUDULENT PRACTICES
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the steps which were taken by the Superintendent of Insurance relating to the North American General Insurance Company already have been put before the house in answer to previous questions. I might add that since receiving information concerning the statement made by Mr. Gruber I asked the Superintendent of Insurance specifically whether he had received such information and what he did about it. I am advised that Mr. Gruber had conversations with Mr. Humphrys, the Superintendent of Insurance, and also with Mr. Brereton, the chief examiner of the department.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: NORTH AMERICAN GENERAL INSURANCE COMPANY-INVESTIGATION RESPECTING COLLAPSE OF COMPANY AND PARTICIPATION IN FRAUDULENT PRACTICES
speechtext: When?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: NORTH AMERICAN GENERAL INSURANCE COMPANY-INVESTIGATION RESPECTING COLLAPSE OF COMPANY AND PARTICIPATION IN FRAUDULENT PRACTICES
speechtext: In January of this year. Mr. Gruber said that he had information to disclose which would be significant to anyone concerned about the affairs of Prudential Finance or its subsidiaries, but would only make the disclosure if he was offered legal protection. It was impossible for the Superintendent of Insurance to offer him legal protection under the law. The Superintendent of Insurance did, not as a result of information given by Mr. Gruber but because the Superintendent of Insurance himself was concerned when the North American General Insurance Company was purchased by Prudential Finance-

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: NORTH AMERICAN GENERAL INSURANCE COMPANY-INVESTIGATION RESPECTING COLLAPSE OF COMPANY AND PARTICIPATION IN FRAUDULENT PRACTICES
speechtext: When was that?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: NORTH AMERICAN GENERAL INSURANCE COMPANY-INVESTIGATION RESPECTING COLLAPSE OF COMPANY AND PARTICIPATION IN FRAUDULENT PRACTICES
speechtext:
I think I gave the information earlier. I do not have it in front of me now, but it is some months ago. The Superintendent of Insurance was concerned at that time about any changes in management practices that

December 16, 1966
Inquiries of the Ministry would take place as a result of the change of ownership. At that time he advised the North American General Insurance Company not to buy or invest in any notes of its parent company, and it never did.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: NORTH AMERICAN GENERAL INSURANCE COMPANY-INVESTIGATION RESPECTING COLLAPSE OF COMPANY AND PARTICIPATION IN FRAUDULENT PRACTICES
speechtext: What about the average Canadian; was there any warning given to him?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: NORTH AMERICAN GENERAL INSURANCE COMPANY-INVESTIGATION RESPECTING COLLAPSE OF COMPANY AND PARTICIPATION IN FRAUDULENT PRACTICES
speechtext: So far as the federal government is concerned its responsibility was only in respect of the North American General Insurance Company.

subtopic: NORTH AMERICAN GENERAL INSURANCE COMPANY-INVESTIGATION RESPECTING COLLAPSE OF COMPANY AND PARTICIPATION IN FRAUDULENT PRACTICES
speechtext: The public be damned.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: NORTH AMERICAN GENERAL INSURANCE COMPANY-INVESTIGATION RESPECTING COLLAPSE OF COMPANY AND PARTICIPATION IN FRAUDULENT PRACTICES
speechtext: It was as a result of the investigations made by the Superintendent of Insurance regarding the change of ownership that a close watch was kept of the affairs of the North American General Insurance Company. It was as a result of that careful watch that a great many special investigations were made, which resulted in the discovery of the theft of securities. There has been no other activity on the part of the North American General Insurance Company which was in any way illegal or contrary to the law. Of course the theft of the securities resulted in the default of the company.

subtopic: NORTH AMERICAN GENERAL INSURANCE COMPANY-INVESTIGATION RESPECTING COLLAPSE OF COMPANY AND PARTICIPATION IN FRAUDULENT PRACTICES
speechtext: I have a supplementary question, Mr. Speaker, which I should like to direct to the acting minister of national revenue or the Minister of Finance. What action did the government take as a result of information received last January in respect of specific allegations of fraud involving $2 million and frauds in respect of income tax laws and bankruptcy proceedings?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: NORTH AMERICAN GENERAL INSURANCE COMPANY-INVESTIGATION RESPECTING COLLAPSE OF COMPANY AND PARTICIPATION IN FRAUDULENT PRACTICES
speechtext: Perhaps I can answer the question on behalf of the Minister of National Revenue.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: NORTH AMERICAN GENERAL INSURANCE COMPANY-INVESTIGATION RESPECTING COLLAPSE OF COMPANY AND PARTICIPATION IN FRAUDULENT PRACTICES
speechtext: You had better consult him.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: NORTH AMERICAN GENERAL INSURANCE COMPANY-INVESTIGATION RESPECTING COLLAPSE OF COMPANY AND PARTICIPATION IN FRAUDULENT PRACTICES
speechtext: Mr. Gruber did provide some information to that department. As hon. members know, it is illegal for any officer of the Department of National Revenue to discuss the affairs of any income taxpayer with anyone.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: NORTH AMERICAN GENERAL INSURANCE COMPANY-INVESTIGATION RESPECTING COLLAPSE OF COMPANY AND PARTICIPATION IN FRAUDULENT PRACTICES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, surely in regard to a matter which involves the loss of millions of dollars the minister is not going to hide behind the question as to whether an income tax revelation was made. Was evidence of fraud given by Mr. Gruber, who had

knowledge of this matter, and what action did the government take between the months of January and September or October, when information was available about this theft?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: NORTH AMERICAN GENERAL INSURANCE COMPANY-INVESTIGATION RESPECTING COLLAPSE OF COMPANY AND PARTICIPATION IN FRAUDULENT PRACTICES
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I do not think the right hon. gentleman would wish to suggest that there are any circumstances under which an officer of the income tax branch should discuss the affairs of any income taxpayer with anyone else. I have heard the right hon. gentleman defend that principle on a number of occasions.

subtopic: NORTH AMERICAN GENERAL INSURANCE COMPANY-INVESTIGATION RESPECTING COLLAPSE OF COMPANY AND PARTICIPATION IN FRAUDULENT PRACTICES
speechtext: Answer the question.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: NORTH AMERICAN GENERAL INSURANCE COMPANY-INVESTIGATION RESPECTING COLLAPSE OF COMPANY AND PARTICIPATION IN FRAUDULENT PRACTICES
speechtext: That is just a smokescreen, Mr. Speaker. I would like the minister to indicate what the Department of National Revenue and the bankruptcy division did after the message was received in January from Mr. Gruber to protect Canadians against the possible loss of money as a result of frauds that were revealed by Mr. Gruber.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: NORTH AMERICAN GENERAL INSURANCE COMPANY-INVESTIGATION RESPECTING COLLAPSE OF COMPANY AND PARTICIPATION IN FRAUDULENT PRACTICES
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I am satisfied, so far as my responsibilities as Minister of Finance are concerned, that every precaution was taken to make sure that companies under our jurisdiction did not act in an illegal way. I am confident that the Superintendent of Insurance did everything he could to protect the positions of the policy and shareholders of this company.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: NORTH AMERICAN GENERAL INSURANCE COMPANY-INVESTIGATION RESPECTING COLLAPSE OF COMPANY AND PARTICIPATION IN FRAUDULENT PRACTICES
speechtext: What did he do?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: NORTH AMERICAN GENERAL INSURANCE COMPANY-INVESTIGATION RESPECTING COLLAPSE OF COMPANY AND PARTICIPATION IN FRAUDULENT PRACTICES
speechtext: So far as income tax information is concerned, I do not think there are any circumstances under which the affairs of a taxpayer should be discussed with anyone, either a member of the government or anybody else.

subtopic: NORTH AMERICAN GENERAL INSURANCE COMPANY-INVESTIGATION RESPECTING COLLAPSE OF COMPANY AND PARTICIPATION IN FRAUDULENT PRACTICES
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, my question is supplementary, but perhaps it should be directed to the Minister of Justice. Is it not a fact that Mr. Gruber, who was an accountant, informed the Superintendent of Bankruptcy in January about his allegations regarding wholesale fraud and losses affecting this particular company? What action was taken by the Department of Justice or the Superintendent of Bankruptcy in regard to these allegations?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: NORTH AMERICAN GENERAL INSURANCE COMPANY-INVESTIGATION RESPECTING COLLAPSE OF COMPANY AND PARTICIPATION IN FRAUDULENT PRACTICES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, there have been several allegations of pre-bankruptcy fraud during the year. I am not sure whether Mr. Gruber actually made an allegation in this particular case. If he did, I am absolutely convinced that
December 16, 1966

the Superintendent of Bankruptcy would have taken all necessary steps to avoid any such incident.

subtopic: NORTH AMERICAN GENERAL INSURANCE COMPANY-INVESTIGATION RESPECTING COLLAPSE OF COMPANY AND PARTICIPATION IN FRAUDULENT PRACTICES
speechtext: What did he do?

subtopic: NORTH AMERICAN GENERAL INSURANCE COMPANY-INVESTIGATION RESPECTING COLLAPSE OF COMPANY AND PARTICIPATION IN FRAUDULENT PRACTICES
speechtext: A further supplementary, Mr. Speaker. Will the Minister of Justice inquire, if he does not know, just exactly what information was given to the Superintendent of Bankruptcy in January by Mr. Gruber, and what action, if any, was in fact taken?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: NORTH AMERICAN GENERAL INSURANCE COMPANY-INVESTIGATION RESPECTING COLLAPSE OF COMPANY AND PARTICIPATION IN FRAUDULENT PRACTICES
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, if Mr. Gruber did give any information, I would be happy to report it to the house.

subtopic: NORTH AMERICAN GENERAL INSURANCE COMPANY-INVESTIGATION RESPECTING COLLAPSE OF COMPANY AND PARTICIPATION IN FRAUDULENT PRACTICES
speechtext: A supplementary question, Mr. Speaker. Did not Mr. Gruber, in January of 1966 inform the minister and the Superintendent of Bankruptcy, over whom the minister had jurisdiction at the time, that several cheques of a fraudulent nature had been written by officials of Prudential for half a million dollars each? If the minister felt this did not fall within his jurisdiction or that of the Superintendent of Bankruptcy, did he have any discussions with or pass that information on to the Attorney General for Ontario?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: NORTH AMERICAN GENERAL INSURANCE COMPANY-INVESTIGATION RESPECTING COLLAPSE OF COMPANY AND PARTICIPATION IN FRAUDULENT PRACTICES
speechtext: I do not know whether Mr. Gruber made any allegation to the Superintendent of Bankruptcy, but it did not come to my attention.

subtopic: NORTH AMERICAN GENERAL INSURANCE COMPANY-INVESTIGATION RESPECTING COLLAPSE OF COMPANY AND PARTICIPATION IN FRAUDULENT PRACTICES
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, 1 have a supplementary question for the Prime Minister. Following all the statements and troubles we have had with fraudulent bankruptcies in the country, including this most recent one, in view of the whole situation does the Prime Minister contemplate having a royal commission inquire into this subject matter as soon as possible?

speakerposition: Prime Minister
subtopic: NORTH AMERICAN GENERAL INSURANCE COMPANY-INVESTIGATION RESPECTING COLLAPSE OF COMPANY AND PARTICIPATION IN FRAUDULENT PRACTICES
speechtext: No, Mr. Speaker; I do not think a royal commission would be helpful in the circumstances.

subtopic: NORTH AMERICAN GENERAL INSURANCE COMPANY-INVESTIGATION RESPECTING COLLAPSE OF COMPANY AND PARTICIPATION IN FRAUDULENT PRACTICES
speechtext: have a supplementary question, Mr. Speaker. The Minister of Finance has said that the Superintendent of Insurance discovered the theft of some half a million dollars of securities from the North American General Insurance Company. When did the Superintendent of Insurance discover this theft?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: NORTH AMERICAN GENERAL INSURANCE COMPANY-INVESTIGATION RESPECTING COLLAPSE OF COMPANY AND PARTICIPATION IN FRAUDULENT PRACTICES
speechtext:
In November, Mr. Speaker. He made an inspection in September, and everything was in order. The theft apparently occurred in the month of October. He discovered it early in November.
Inquiries of the Ministry

subtopic: NORTH AMERICAN GENERAL INSURANCE COMPANY-INVESTIGATION RESPECTING COLLAPSE OF COMPANY AND PARTICIPATION IN FRAUDULENT PRACTICES
speechtext: A supplementary question, Mr. Speaker. I would ask the Minister of Finance the nature of the protection or immunity asked for by Mr. Gruber, and did he say why he felt he required it? Of what was he afraid?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: NORTH AMERICAN GENERAL INSURANCE COMPANY-INVESTIGATION RESPECTING COLLAPSE OF COMPANY AND PARTICIPATION IN FRAUDULENT PRACTICES
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I am advised that he felt legal action might be taken against him by third parties.

subtopic: NORTH AMERICAN GENERAL INSURANCE COMPANY-INVESTIGATION RESPECTING COLLAPSE OF COMPANY AND PARTICIPATION IN FRAUDULENT PRACTICES
speechtext: In what respect?

subtopic: NORTH AMERICAN GENERAL INSURANCE COMPANY-INVESTIGATION RESPECTING COLLAPSE OF COMPANY AND PARTICIPATION IN FRAUDULENT PRACTICES
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I should like to ask a question supplementary to the one asked by the hon. member for Kamloops. I direct my question to the Minister of Finance. Is it the minister's information that Mr. Gruber was in fact the auditor for the Prudential and that group of companies?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: NORTH AMERICAN GENERAL INSURANCE COMPANY-INVESTIGATION RESPECTING COLLAPSE OF COMPANY AND PARTICIPATION IN FRAUDULENT PRACTICES

speakeroldname: Right Hon. J. G. Diefenbaker (Leader of the Opposition):
speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: NORTH AMERICAN GENERAL INSURANCE COMPANY-INVESTIGATION RESPECTING COLLAPSE OF COMPANY AND PARTICIPATION IN FRAUDULENT PRACTICES
speechtext: I have a supplementary question, Mr. Speaker. This matter cannot be brushed aside quite as easily as the minister is attempting to do. speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: NORTH AMERICAN GENERAL INSURANCE COMPANY-INVESTIGATION RESPECTING COLLAPSE OF COMPANY AND PARTICIPATION IN FRAUDULENT PRACTICES

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: NORTH AMERICAN GENERAL INSURANCE COMPANY-INVESTIGATION RESPECTING COLLAPSE OF COMPANY AND PARTICIPATION IN FRAUDULENT PRACTICES

I shall have to add this word, however. I do not think it would be appropriate for any minister to table correspondence that would reveal the income tax position of any taxpayer in this country. On the second point, the question of responsibility is divided here between the federal and the provincial governments. The real issue here, I

December 16, 1966
Inquiries of the Ministry regret to say, is that the laws of Ontario do not protect the investors and the policy holders of provincial companies as well as they should.

subtopic: NORTH AMERICAN GENERAL INSURANCE COMPANY-INVESTIGATION RESPECTING COLLAPSE OF COMPANY AND PARTICIPATION IN FRAUDULENT PRACTICES
speechtext: Hear, hear.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: NORTH AMERICAN GENERAL INSURANCE COMPANY-INVESTIGATION RESPECTING COLLAPSE OF COMPANY AND PARTICIPATION IN FRAUDULENT PRACTICES
speechtext: We are talking about the dominion laws, laws administered by this department, the department represented by the Minister of Finance. We are asking what you are going to do about it? subtopic: NORTH AMERICAN GENERAL INSURANCE COMPANY-INVESTIGATION RESPECTING COLLAPSE OF COMPANY AND PARTICIPATION IN FRAUDULENT PRACTICES
speechtext: Accept your responsibility.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: NORTH AMERICAN GENERAL INSURANCE COMPANY-INVESTIGATION RESPECTING COLLAPSE OF COMPANY AND PARTICIPATION IN FRAUDULENT PRACTICES
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I have made it quite clear that I take full responsibility as far as the administrative responsibility of the federal government is concerned, and that relates at the present time to federally incorporated insurance companies. speakeroldname: Hon. Robert Winters (Minister of Trade and Commerce):
speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce

speechtext:
Yesterday the hon. member for Nanaimo-Cowichan-The Islands (Mr. Cameron) asked a question about a report received from Washington that the United States administration is issuing or has issued new guide lines which would affect subsidiaries of United States corporations in Canada in import and export positions. I shall be glad to answer that question, though, in so far as it applies to financial institutions perhaps it should be referred to the Minister of Finance.
The answer is that the United States administration has issued new guide lines with respect to direct foreign investment by United States corporations applicable to the two year period 1966-67, similar in form to the guide lines issued about a year ago for the period 1965-66. Following the announcement of the United States guideline program about a year ago, Canadian ministers attending the joint United States-Canadian committee on trade and economic affairs held in March, 1966, sought clarification of the intent of the program and were given assurance that the guide lines were not intended to interfere with normal business practice. The existence of these guide lines during the past year did not interfere with the realization in Canada of a substantially larger capital investment program.
Yesterday in Washington I discussed with Mr. Connor, Secretary of Commerce, the revised guide lines applicable to the 1966-67 period. Mr. Chairman, I want to make a few comments in respect of the amendment, and explain the attitude of the government in putting the provision in the bill confining the income supplement to pensioners born on or before December 31, 1910.
As hon. members may recall, the Senate committee recommended a program of income maintenance to be applied to old age pensioners. One of the changes we made in the proposal of the Senate committee was to limit the application of the supplement to those pensioners born in 1910 or earlier. We carefully considered the relationship of permanence, in contrast to a transitional program, to the role of the Canada Pension Plan.
Members of the committee will recall that the joint committee on the Canada Pension Plan and the Senate committee on aging expressed concern about those people who were too old to benefit from the Canada Pension Plan. We assumed, and still do, that the main retirement program for the people of Canada was the Canada Pension Plan, which is based upon contributions from both employees and employers. The supplement therefore is intended to serve as a transitional measure, while the contributory retirement pension program is maturing.
This supplement will be payable to those current and future old age security recipients who, by reason of age alone, will be unable to benefit substantially from the provisions of the Canada or Quebec pension plans. That is the rationale behind the approach put forward in this bill.
It was pointed out in statements last night that there will be a group of persons born after 1910 who for one reason or other will not have an opportunity, to participate in the Canada or Quebec pension plans. We believe that such a group will be relatively small and we doubt whether a parallel income support program should be developed strictly for application to this particular group, especially in view of the fact this house passed the Canada
December IS, 1SS8
Assistance Plan which can be used as a program for general public assistance. The Canada Assistance Plan also provides health and welfare benefits.
The hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam expressed some concern about the coverage of the Canada Pension Plan. The fact is, of course, that the Canada Pension Plan provides comprehensive coverage. It is in fact one of the most comprehensive contributory programs of its kind. It does cover farmers and fishermen. In respect of housewives, as referred to by the hon. member, our approach has been to provide a combined pension for the husband and the wife so that the wife can derive a bigger pension should the husband die. It should be borne in mind that many housewives will be contributors in their own right and will derive benefits, as well as the income support, because their husbands have been contributors.
Hon. members may not agree with what I am saying about the relationship of this program to the Canada Pension Plan. I do not object to that, but I should like to communicate my concern about a permanent parallel program of income support in connection with the Canada Pension Plan. That is precisely why this program is transitional in nature. I want to point out two things to the minister. The first is that he can resolve that problem very easily by incorporating this $30 in the basic old age security pension. There would be no feeling of injury then from 1975, on, if those who had contributed to the Canada Pension Plan knew that in addition to their entitlement under that legislation they were also entitled to a basic pension of $100 or $105 a month. This is why we have been arguing that this money, which the government is now proposing to pay, be incorporated into the old age security pension.
What the government are really doing-and it is becoming more transparent day by day-is really to fix $75 a month, plus whatever additional increments will come as a result of the increased cost of living, as a permanent feature of our social security legislation. This will mean that from now on $75 a month plus 75 cents a month for a 1 per cent increase in the cost of living, with a maximum of $1.50 for 2 percentage points, irrespective of whether the cost of living rises by 3 per cent, 4 per cent or more, will be fixed as the basic pension of the old age security pensioner. In many instances it will not even keep pace with the increased cost of living, let alone allow our elderly citizens in this country to participate in the nation's increased productivity. The old age security pension is now fixed, as I say, except for the increment arising out of the increased cost of living.
I am sure that when the government introduced the Canada Pension Plan it was not apparent to most Canadians that the old age security pension was being frozen, except for the cost of living bonus. But it is now perfectly apparent that it has been frozen. It is also apparent that the measure now before us is not going to be the basis of a universally guaranteed annual income. If we are to show decency and generosity at Christmastime the minister ought to accept the request I shall make in the terms of an amendment.
If hon. members look at new section 7, subclause 2, paragraph Cc) they will discover that pensioners outside Canada, away from the country for more than six months, are not entitled to draw the supplement or the so-called guaranteed income payment.
I am pleading the case of not many people, though many seem to write to me. I am strenuously pleading the case of people who have no vote in this country, who have moved to warmer climates in the south or to the United Kingdom. They do not vote in Canadian general elections. To me this is all the more reason for doing the fair, decent and generous thing.
Old Age Security Act Amendment
As hon. members know, it has taken us a long time to get the Old Age Security Act amended to make it possible for people who find it necessary or desirable to live somewhere else to draw the old age security pension. We finally achieved this in two jumps. In the first place we provided some years ago that a person qualified for a pension in Canada, who has started drawing it while living in Canada, may go anywhere in the world and continue drawing that pension provided he had lived in Canada for 25 years subsequent to his twenty first birthday. That provision was enacted some years ago, and it was a good one.
More recently when dealing with the legislation enacting the Canada Pension Plan we made another improvement. We looked at the person who has had to leave Canada before attaining pensionable age. He may have had many years of residence in this country; he may have been born in this country, but he was denied the pension unless he came back and lived here for another 12 months.
The kinds of cases coming under this heading surely are well known to hon. members. For example there will be the case of a man and his wife, the man being of pensionable age and his wife not. They go to England; the man gets his pension but the wife cannot because she went there before she was of pensionable age. Or there are single persons moving about for one reason or another, going to various places, the most common of which would be the southern parts of this continent. We resolved the problem of the person who cannot get back to the country by another provision now in the act under which, if a person had a total of 40 years residence in Canada subsequent to age 18, he need not come back to this country to get his pension. I have already come across sad cases of people who are a few weeks short of the required 40 years. I recall the case of one woman who was born in this country, as her parents were born in this country, but who cannot qualify because she is two or three months short of that 40 year period. I do not intend to go into these provisions. I merely indicate that we have made them. It was difficult to get this concession, and the qualifications are difficult to meet. But the concession has been made. Now, by this provision in subsection (2) of section 7, we say that even though people have met the qualification and
11240	COMMONS
Old Age Security Act Amendment are drawing the basic pension in, for example, the southern states, or in England, they cannot get the supplement.
Mr. Chairman, how mean can we be? How unthoughtful can we be? Some might argue that if these people have been able to go away, they have resources. Well, if they have resources they would not get the supplement in any case under this legislation. But if a person is entitled to a pension on the basis of the 25-year clause or the 40-year, and needs a supplement, I think he should get it.
I am not trying to set people against each other when 1 point out how unfair the present discrimination can be. Please note that a person who did not come to this country until he was 54 or 55 can get a pension in ten years time. And if he stays here he can get a supplement, provided he meets the means test incorporated in this bill. I am in favour of that; let that be clear. But it does seem odd that a person who has been in this country ten years can draw the $105 if he needs it, while another, who may have been born in this country and lived here for 58 years, cannot get a supplement because he has gone to England or some other part of the world. It seems to me that this is unfair and that it is carrying the unChristmas spirit a little too far.
The minister told us in the speech he made that this provision had been included in the bill deliberately. I feel strongly that it should come out. We have made it possible for those people who have to go away, and who meet the various conditions, to get a pension. They should have a right to get the supplement as well. For the most part we are concerned with people whose health in their latter years does not permit them to endure our winters. Or they are people who have moved to other parts of the world for family reasons-to live with relatives, and so on.
I am not talking about the millionaires the minister seems concerned about. If the millionaires have gone to California, they cannot beat the means test. But having found the answer as far as the basic old age pension is concerned we should not make it impossible for pensioners to receive the supplement because they are living elsewhere. I urge the minister not to give us a long song and dance telling us why this cannot be done. My flies upstairs are full of letters from the previous minister, from the hon. member for Perth, when he was minister, from the Secretary of State for External Affairs, when he was minister of health and welfare, explaining how difficult it was to make pensions payable to

speechtext:
I can say to the committee that the Chair has considered this amendment in the light of the resolution which preceded the bill. I have paid particular attention to the statement made by the Minister of National Health and Welfare, and the meaning which he places upon the word "certain."
Old Age Security Act Amendment
It is the opinion of the Chair that while this word "certain" does impose some limit, it is a limit which is defined in the bill; and since the limit is defined in the bill, then to change the limit in the bill, or to express certain limits, does not at all do any violence to the resolution preceding the bill. The word "certain" may have limitations. The bill states what these limitations are. But I do not think the committee is bound by the limitations placed upon the word "certain" by the bill itself.
I would like to read again from Beau-chesne's fourth edition citation 278(4);
The committee is not bound by the terms of the provisions which the ministers have inserted in the bill; and, when no amount has been mentioned m the resolution, any member may propose to increase the grants specified in the bill or to extend the application of the provisions of the bill, whatever may be the cost resulting therefrom, so long as the power conferred by the royal recommendation is not exceeded.
It is my opinion that this amendment does not exceed the royal recommendation, and I would therefore rule that the amendment is in order.

subtopic: PROVISION OF GUARANTEED INCOME SUPPLEMENTS AND DETERMINATION OF PENSIONERS' INCOMES
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, just before you made your ruling I said that I found it difficult to understand the reasoning and the point of view which the minister is taking with regard to this amendment. As I said, he was referred to earlier in debate as a Scrooge. I am not going to repeat the long arguments and discussions we have had on the principle of whether $30 a month should apply to all people who are entitled to the old age pension, or just to those who can satisfy the needs test. This has been debated for days. We have had a number of votes in which the house and the committee have expressed their points of view. We on this side of the chamber disagree with the government and with the minister, but that decision has been made.
However, Mr. Chairman, surely the number of people covered by this amendment is so small, and the reasons this small group of people leave the country are so valid, that the government does not have to drive the last nail into the coffin. This is not a new question. It took many years argument before the government of Canada agreed that any old age pensioner who left the country could get a pension. Finally, some years ago, it was agreed that people who qualified could draw their pension, regardless of where they lived.
There are not many of these people. As the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre has already said, those who have left the country

11242	COMMONS
Old Age Security Act Amendment have done it mainly for two reasons. One is a health reason. I have just come back from my home city of Winnipeg where the people have had a month of below zero weather. It is no wonder that some people who are in their late sixties and seventies find it difficult to live in Winnipeg during the winter, and think it a good idea to go down to the United States, or some other place, where the conditions are easier for them to live. I also know some people, the bulk of whose relatives have already died, but they have brothers or sisters down in the United States, or in Great Britain. They have decided it would be easier and more pleasant for them to finish the last few years of their lives in close association with those brothers or sisters.
These are valid reasons which were recognized by the government of Canada and the parliament of Canada when the pension legislation was amended to permit people to live outside Canada and still draw their pension. But now the minister comes along and says, "Well, that is all right for the people who get the $75 a month. They can live in the United States, they can live in Great Britain or anywhere else, but they cannot get this supplementary benefit."
I cannot see any logic behind this and, as I said at the beginning of my remarks, I wish the minister would stop thinking of this bill as being like the Ten Commandments tablets which cannot be changed under any circumstances, and that he would exhibit some of the compassion which some hon. members and some people throughout the country thought he had, but which he is rapidly demonstrating he does not have.

[Mr. Orlikow.l

Dealing with the merits of the amendment I would point out to the minister that obviously the number of people involved will not be large. The old age pensioners who can go abroad on either $75 a month, or on a maximum of $105 a month, is not going to be substantial. If they have not already made their pile to go and live in Spain or Florida during the harsher months of the year, they are never going to make it.
I suggest that the type of person who will take advantage of this will be somebody who, in any event, is helped by his or her family to move to a softer clime so as not to experience the great Canadian winter. I further suggest that the families of such people are making considerable sacrifices, and that these sacrifices are being made only for one purpose, for the health of their relatives who find it necessary to move to milder climates.
[DOT] (1:30 p.m.)

So, I should like to end where I started; there were two Scrooges, the miserable fellow at the beginning of the Dickens story and that kind, benevolent soul who emerged after an exhausting ordeal-

subtopic: PROVISION OF GUARANTEED INCOME SUPPLEMENTS AND DETERMINATION OF PENSIONERS' INCOMES
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, it has been acknowledged by all Canadians that the old age security pension is an entitlement to the people who have contributed toward the growth of the nation. It is quite clear from the minister and the government that this supplement is not considered as a right. By virtue of this provision the government has discretion to decide which of these senior citizens, having complied with all the requirements of the old age security provisions, shall be entitled to this supplement. In order to point out the anomaly, I should like to make a comparison to the situation in respect of the Canada Pension Plan. Under the Canada Pension Plan a person can move here from some other country. He can live here for ten years, take
December 16, 1966	COMMONS DEBATES	11243
his full Canada Pension Plan, and then go back to the place from which he came. Hon. members might say: "Oh, yes, but that is a contributory pension plan". The fact is that such a person, particularly if he is earning $5,000 a year or more when he retires, can draw his pension after contributing for ten years only and receive a bonus, an unearned increment, which is paid to him by the other people of Canada to the tune of some $18,000.
On the other hand, under this bill, a person who has lived in Canada for 20 years after age 21-he may have lived here for 40 or 50 years-who on account of health of other reasons wishes to live in some other country is not entitled to the supplement. Perhaps the minister could tell us how many of these people are affected. Will granting the supplement to these people increase the cost in respect of this measure to any appreciable extent? If not, why does the minister take this "Scroogey" attitude in respect of these citizens who have earned a right to the supplement?

subtopic: PROVISION OF GUARANTEED INCOME SUPPLEMENTS AND DETERMINATION OF PENSIONERS' INCOMES
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I should like to make a very earnest appeal to the minister to change his mind in this regard. I wish to do so for several reasons. I think he was wrong in not accepting the earlier amendment which was moved. In that case at least, I think he had some reason which I believe I understood. Unfortunately, somewhat to the shame of Canada, there are people whose income is so low that their pensions under the Canada Pension Plan would not be greater than the supplementary income that the early subclause represented. So, at least he had some reason.
I suggest, with all the earnestness which all of us can possibly muster, that there is no reason for the stand the minister is taking. First, as has been pointed out by other speakers, the number of people who will be able to leave Canada and go elsewhere, having only $75 or $80 a mnth, obviously is exceedingly small. They will be people who are ill or who have children living in Detroit, Rome or in some other place and who wish to spend the remaining few years of their lives with their children and grandchildren. The denial of this supplement to them, to me seems to be an act of inhumanity of which I thought the minister was incapable. I mean both parts of that; it is an act of inhumanity and I would have thought that the minister was incapable of it. How many thousands of dollars are involved in this? I suppose one of the reasons the minister wishes to have this subclause in the
Old Age Security Act Amendment bill is that his officers have persuaded him it would be very difficult to check the forms containing the income returns from people who are resident elsewhere. I should like to say to him in passing that this is another reason to condemn his income test.
Even if this were the case, let me remind him that there are dozens of laws on our books which unfortunately are violated daily by residents and citizens of Canada which the governments, federal and provincial, do not bother to police, because the cost of policing would be greater than the few pennies they would gather as a result of such policing. Everyone knows that. It is unfortunate, but it is a fact. He is not worried about that. Governments are not worried about the little infractions which cost the treasury a few measly thousands of dollars. When the minister suggests that people who have lived most of their lives in Canada who reach the age of 65 eventually and now age 69 or 68, and who find that they would like to spend the remaining few years of their lives with their children and grandchildren somewhere outside Canada, cannot get a pension above the $75 a month under the old age security provisions, this is picayune; it is petty. It is petty in mind and petty in heart, if I may use that term. It represents no money; it represents no principle. It represents a bureaucratic intrusion which has absolutely no basis in fact, logic or anything else.
This attitude represents a sacrifice of simple, human compassion for some kind of procedural difficulty which might occur in respect of some loss of the occasional measly dollar which the treasury might have to endure because a person is out of the country for six months. I am making my statement as others have-and I am not saying that I am any different from the others-not with any intention of embarrassing the minister or the government. From my short experience in parliament, I believe that if we leave the government alone it does enough to embarrass itself. No one on the opposition benches has to aid them in that direction. With all my heart,
I am making the plea to the minister that he realize he is making a mistake. He is making a mistake of pettiness for which he will be branded as the Scrooge which people have called him, just as his department will be branded as a department without imagination and without heart.
If the minister could tell us how many thousands of dollars this will cost the treasury of Canada or if he could tell us what it is he is
December 16, 1966

Old Age Security Act Amendment trying to protect himself against, I would be glad to listen to him. However, I have applied my mind to this matter and my experience in respect of the older people in this country, which probably is as wide as that of anyone else, and for the life of me I cannot see why, when the old age pensioner is entitled to receive the old age security pension when he is beyond the boundaries of this country, this little addition of $30 a month-and it might be less-should be denied him. The only explanation I can see is that some officers in his department must have advised him concerning the procedural difficulty there would be in respect of checking the applications and so on. So what? So, you cannot check them.
[DOT] (1:40 p.m.)

subtopic: PROVISION OF GUARANTEED INCOME SUPPLEMENTS AND DETERMINATION OF PENSIONERS' INCOMES
speechtext: It is to be a very simple form.

subtopic: PROVISION OF GUARANTEED INCOME SUPPLEMENTS AND DETERMINATION OF PENSIONERS' INCOMES
speechtext:
It may well be a simple form, but a person who pays no taxes may have difficulty. My question is, so what? Out of 1,200,000 pensioners, which is the number there are now, I should like to know how many in fact live abroad. This whole question does not involve only how many live abroad, because there might be very many pensioners out of the country. The $75 is paid as a matter of right even to those who can afford to go abroad. I want to know whether the minister really thinks there is a substantial number, significant number or even a small number of pensioners who are living outside of the country and do not receive at least $105 per month in income. It is absurd to suggest that there is a crack in the wall of financial responsibility in this regard which would cause any embarrassment or any loss worth a tinker's damn.
Often the minister does accept advice, yet in this case he has a certain approach to legislation which leads him to bring in this kind of petty, mean provision which is what it is. It is a petty, mean provision of no consequence to the country, of no consequence to the treasury, but of consequence only to a few thousand people who will be living with their children or grandchildren outside this country. Those are the few who will benefit from this additional pittance provided by this bill. I appeal to the minister to recognize the validity of the representations made by hon. members on this side of the house in order to show that he has some understanding of, if I may say this without any offence, the workings of a genuine democratic legislature or assembly where a minister does not simply put legislation on the desk

and say we must accept it. In a democratic assembly the minister and the government have sufficient humility from time to time to accept propositions from those who oppose them, given in good faith and in all sincerity. If the minister does not accept this amendment which does no violence to the principles of the act and no violence to anything else which is of consequence, I can only conclude that he is becoming-I have not known him long enough to say that he has been-the kind of administrator who is more bound by his bureaucratic fears than he is by his principles as a human being.

subtopic: PROVISION OF GUARANTEED INCOME SUPPLEMENTS AND DETERMINATION OF PENSIONERS' INCOMES

As I look upon the minister's mournful countenance, I wonder whether he regards us as being unseemingly persistent in pressing forward this amendment. If the minister is really anxious to press forward with greater speed and expedition, it seems to me he should be prepared to give us some concrete, statistical information as to the cost involved in the proposition before us. I suspect, because I have not seen any figure, that what is involved by way of additional cost is not of any great magnitude. If that is the case I should like to say to members opposite and to the minister that if we must choose between administrative stringency on the one hand and the generosity of Canadian society on the other, we ought to choose the latter. One must be prudent in dealing with measures of this kind, but if there is a very substantial cost factor involved there is an onus on the minister to bring forward concrete statistical information to indicate the range of additional cost involved in the proposal suggested by this amendment.
I might say that I also regard the provision in subclause (a) as being unnecessarily stringent. If I were to speak about that provision at this point I would be out of order so I shall defer my remarks until after we have dealt with this amendment.

Mr. Chairman, I rise to speak to the committee with great diffidence after the avalanche of unpleasant adjectives that have been thrown at me in respect of this amendment.
First of all, we kept in mind the fact that this supplement will be paid in all cases for the month a pensioner leaves Canada and for a maximum of an additional six consecutive months. Payment will be stopped at that time,

Old Age Security Act Amendment
but will be resumed the month the pensioner returns to Canada.
The hon. member for Halifax and others made allusions to what had been done in the past by former ministers. The policy being followed in this case is precisely the policy applied to pensioners receiving the basic $75 a month who have left the country and have not put in 25 years residence after age 21. That is a provision of the Old Age Security Act. That principle which is included in that act was applied to the supplement payment. A pensioner will get it for the month he leaves Canada and for a maximum of six consecutive months thereafter. If he remains outside the country beyond that period payment will be suspended, but it will be resumed when he returns.

Old Age Security Act Amendment the period of six months. I appreciate their concern. subtopic: PROVISION OF GUARANTEED INCOME SUPPLEMENTS AND DETERMINATION OF PENSIONERS' INCOMES

Would the minister permit another question, Mr. Chairman? When he says he is following what is in the law now, he should distinguish between those people who claim their pension on the basis of only 10 years' residence and who therefore when they go abroad cannot draw the pension continuously, and those people who go abroad after having had 25 years in Canada subsequent to age 21, or went abroad before they became recipients of the pension with 40 years residence in Canada subsequent to age 18. I am talking about these two groups of people, the 25-year group and the 40-year group, with respect to whom we have said they can have the $75 pension. No matter whether they are living in the affluent United States, where they have a social security scheme, if we give them the $75 and they are in need, why cannot they receive the supplement? I plead with the minister not to confuse the issue about the 25-year and the 40-year groups by talking about what applies in the case of the 10-year group.
My amendment would not give this supplement to those people with only 10 years residence in Canada who stay abroad beyond six months, because they do not get the $75. That was quite a long question, Mr. Chairman. Mr. Chairman, I think the hon. member is suggesting the complexity of the administrative operation in making these benefits available. I am not arguing against the concern of hon. members; I am arguing
December 16, 1966	COMMONS
about the difficulty of trying to administer the program and establish equity between persons resident in Canada and those resident abroad. They can be abroad up to six months and draw this supplement. If they come back they will immediately go on benefit. These people are living in 60 different countries. There are 1,000 pensioners living in Hong Kong. We just cannot possibly hope to administer the program in any effective way and relate 60 different countries, with different income standards, when this program is geared to our own Canadian income level. It seems to me the committee is asking me to undertake something that is almost impossible to accomplish effectively. I do not want to argue against the concern of hon. members of the committee, but I would like the committee to understand the difficulty their suggestion presents and with which I am asked to deal.

subtopic: PROVISION OF GUARANTEED INCOME SUPPLEMENTS AND DETERMINATION OF PENSIONERS' INCOMES
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, the minister has let the large cat out of the bag. It is not a question of the spirit of this legislation or the intent of what we are trying to do for Canadians, whether they live at home or abroad; but rather it is a question of how such an amendment to the Old Age Security Act could be administered. The minister has spoken about administrative difficulties. This is a point that many of us suspected was really in his mind when he opposed this very reasonable suggestion. days in which, every time the parties wanted to woo the votes of the older citizens of Canada, they attempted to outbid each other and insulted the senior citizens by saying, in effect, that their votes were worth so many dollars to the party. speechtext:
This is probably the most clumsily drafted bill ever presented in this house. This is also the opinion of a number of people who are trained to draft bills of this kind. We should return to the principle of drafting bills which communicate their purpose to hon. members of this house.
I intend to move an amendment to assist those people in Canada who are over 65 years of age but who did not go past the third or fourth grade in school. They experienced two world wars and a great depression. They are now faced with increasing automation. This group comprises approximately 150,000 people in Canada. They have little income but are physically and mentally able to work. I refer to these people who do casual work such as gardening, cutting lawns, shovelling snow, babysitting, sewing and perhaps cleaning. These people earn in the neighbourhood of $400 to $800 per year. They do not keep books. They are faced with the necessity of paying their carfare to get to their jobs and buying

tools and extra clothing. These people are happy to perform these small tasks and they are assisting the economy of this country.
As a result of the provisions of this measure we will be forcing these people to stay at home rather than work. They require transportation, extra boots, extra clothing and in some cases, tools. As a result of these necessary expenses they will find that by working they are money out of pocket. These people will find it cheaper to stay at home sitting on the front porch in the summer and watching television in the winter, if they can afford a television set. We are destroying these people mentally and physically. If they stay at home and do nothing they will degenerate to the point where they will have to be taken care of in homes or hospitals. One can find many of these people in our institutions. These people have not had the opportunity of earning very much during their lives and I ask the minister to give them some consideration.
By the provisions of this bill we will be doing a great disservice to those Canadians who for health purposes leave Canada on the advice of their doctors. There is a tremendous increase in the number of elderly Canadians who suffer from respiratory diseases such as emphysema, bronchitis and asthma. By discriminating against these people we are being penny wise and pound foolish.
In order to provide some opportunity for these people to obtain happiness I move:
That subsection (1) of new section 8 of clause 3 be amended by the addition of the following proviso thereto:
'Provided that no deduction shall be made in the case of a single person having earned less than three hundred and sixty dollars in the preceding year and in the case of a married person, otherwise qualified, having earned less than seven hundred and twenty dollars in the preceding year.'

Mr. Chairman, I, too, indicated yesterday that I had an amendment that I wished to propose to the new Section 8, subsection (1), being enacted by clause 3 of Bill No. C-251. It is not necessary for me to restate at any length our basic position with regard to this legislation, but it does seem to me that the validity of our position has been strengthened as this debate has continued. Our position is that we welcome wholeheartedly the proposal to raise the amount available as an old age security pension in this country to $105 a month, but at the same time we fee] that amount should be paid across the board. We are therefore opposed to any test of income, by whatever name it might be called, that denies to some of our senior citizens the full amount of that pension.
As the debate has continued, it has brought out the fact that the complications in connection with this program are going to be numerous. It has brought out the fact that the differences that will be established among people will be most unfair. I think that by now the Minister of National Health and Welfare
Old Age Security Act Amendment should be persuaded that it would have been far better in the first place to have brought in a straight, across the board increase to $105 a month. I, therefore, rise now to give him the opportunity to consider this proposition again. It is not too late to make the kind of Christmas present to our senior citizens that would really be appreciated; and I do not have in mind the kind of celebration for Christmas that the Minister of Finance suggested out on the west coast the other night.
The new section 8 provides for a supplement to be paid on top of the $75, which for the year 1967 would be $30 and for any year after that would be 40 per cent of the amount of the old age security pension. That reference to 40 per cent in the case of years after 1967 of course takes into account the fact that the basic $75 may be increased by a maximum of $1.50 a year if the cost of living index rises by 2 per cent in each year. But the provision of this total package of $105 a month to pensioners is qualified by a test which is to be found in the first three lines on page 3 of the bill.
I think that test should be removed. Perhaps I may for a moment refer to the arguments the minister advanced when he did not like the fact we were asking that this legislation be extended and made permanent. I am sure he knew then that it was our view that not only should the legislation be made permanent but that it should be without a means test. As far as we are concerned, these two propositions go together.
Therefore, Mr. Chairman, in order to give the minister an opportunity once again to consider removing the test and making this $30 increase an across the board improvement in the pension, I move:
That clause 3 of Bill C-251 be amended by deleting from sub-section (1) of the new section 8 being enacted thereby, the words "minus one dollar for each two full dollars of his monthly base income, being one-twelfth of his income for the preceding year", as found in lines 1, 2, and 3 on page 3 of the bill.
[DOT] (3:10 p.m.)
So as to be clear, Mr. Chairman, if this amendment is accepted it would remove the test and make the $30 increase in 1967, and the 40 per cent of whatever the basic pension is after that, across the board without the kind of means or income test that is presently in the bill.

I would be happy to oblige the hon. lady and try to clarify the situation. There are two aspects of this problem. The first is: how do we treat supplementary assistance payments made by the province of British Columbia? Well, those are not reported as income for our purposes. They are excluded because they are not included in the definition of income under the Income Tax Act. So, an applicant from British Columbia
Old Age Security Act Amendment receiving assistance in 1966 and applying to us would not be obliged to include that amount as income.
[DOT] (3:40 p.m.)
Therefore, the benefit being received from the province of British Columbia would not disqualify the person, or reduce in any way the benefit available from this program. Our definition of income is such that a person in receipt of that assistance supplement in British Columbia, is not disqualified.
The second point raised by the hon. member for Comox-Alberni has to do with the amount of any pension or supplement, and the amount of any similar payment under the law of a provincial legislature or of the parliament of Canada. The effect of that amendment would be to do something which is already done under the law because we could not include the Old Age Security pension, and the supplement, as part of income. Therefore, his amendment is totally redundant in that sense.
What we are asking here, which is something different to the point raised by the hon. member for Vancouver-Kingsway, is that if a province pays a pension like the $75 pension, how would we treat it under this program? We provide that it, or any supplement similar to our supplement, would not be treated as income for our purposes. The effect of that is to make it possible for a provincial resident to receive a benefit from a provincial government without losing any benefit under this bill.
There are two different aspects here. There is the aspect with respect to an assistance payment, which is excluded from the definition of income, and there is this direct provision which does not include as income the amount of any pension or supplement, and the amount of any similar payment under the law of a provincial legislature.
The only case in existence in Canada is the $25 payable by the government of Prince Edward Island. It is an across the board $25, above the $75, to every pensioner in Prince Edward Island. Under this provision the recipient of that pension from Prince Edward Island is not disqualified in any sense, so far as we are concerned, from receiving our supplement.

But this new section in this bill opens up the whole field of income and the sources of income of an applicant, and I submit this is a very different thing from the provision which the house agreed to with respect to the administration of the Canada Pension Plan. I take it we are now considering new section 17 of clause 3. When I spoke on this bill two or three days ago I drew attention to this new section and I pointed out that there were nine areas in which the Minister of National Health and Welfare could undertake extra investigation to determine the incomes of applicants for this supplementary pension. He said I was misinterpreting this provision. Nevertheless it was at that stage I said he was going to have snoopers looking into the incomes of old age pensioners.
Now that we are down to a detailed study of new section 17 we find that I was right in my suggestion, that this snooping process is going to take place in an area which heretofore has been considered sacrosanct. This morning the Minister of Finance indicated that income tax forms do fall into this category. It has always been our understanding that no one could look at an income tax form unless there was a special order to do so. A special arrangement is now being made in respect of the Department of National Health and Welfare.
I understood the minister to say that if the house passes this measure authority will be given to investigate income tax forms. For this reason we should resist such action to the greatest extent possible. This is an indirect way of destroying the confidentiality on which people have relied up to this time. The seriousness of this move is now apparent to hon.
Old Age Security Act Amendment members. We should support the amendment and we should do everything in our power to prevent this change in the law. I believe that the suggested change in the law should have been resisted by the Minister of Finance and the Minister of National Revenue. These two people who are responsible for the finances of this country should be the first to object to snoopers in their departments looking at forms which contain confidential information. Alternatively, if snoopers are to be allowed to look at income tax forms filed by pensioners they should be allowed to look at forms filed by companies or corporations.
It is my belief there will be a storm of criticism in this country when the public become aware that the door is being opened to this extent. I doubt that anyone wants his income tax form examined by a casual observer. There are two inherent dangers in this situation. We are putting the stamp of approval on snoopers and we are invading the privacy of the individual. We will be destroying the confidentiality of income tax returns. Let the Minister of Finance tell us whether he thinks this is not a bad move. I believe it is because people will say that the act which amended the Old Age Security Act made it possible for snoopers to investigate income tax returns. They will believe that no serious objection was taken, although the fact is that our objections are always brushed aside. They will believe that this having been done it can be done in the future in respect of other acts. They will believe that we have given approval to this type of investigation.
[DOT] (5:20 p.m.)
In some other bill brought forward in the future we will find a similar provision. Other people will be given the privilege of investigating income tax returns and the whole matter will then be wide open. The time to stop is when the first break appears in the dyke. This is when the hole should be plugged. We would lack diligence in the performance of our duty if we permitted such a provision to go through at any time. This involves more than simply protesting. The whole proposal must be resisted to the very limit. I add my words of objection to this particular section and I will support the amendment proposed by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre.

Mr. Chairman, I want to make a few observations on this matter. I intend to support the amendment. I can do so with consistency because at the time a proposal of a similar nature to that which the government now advances was raised in connection with the Canada Pension Plan I opposed it.
When we examine the type of legislation being introduced by governments now, and this government in particular, with regard to matters of this kind-this was the case with the Canada Pension Plan-we find that all too often the principle governing the immemorial right of a person who may be charged with any offence, namely, to be convicted only as and when evidence is produced by the crown to establish his guilt, is being altered. There is in this proposal which the government advances, as in other cases, the suggestion that evidence can be obtained from other sources, government documents and government records, on the basis of which people can be convicted by statements which they themselves have made and which were made on the basis that they were privileged and not subject to inspection.
I th:nk the amendment is one that should be supported. I believe there should be no doubt, having in mind the provisions of the section which provides for the establishment of offences and punishments, that the committee should support the amendment. In view of the remarks that have been made, this section should not be allowed to pass in its present form. Surely the onus lies upon the government to justify their attempt to establish this extraordinary power. They do not successfully discharge that onus merely by saying, "We did it once before". I do not care whether this government or any government did it before. It is an extraordinary remedy that they are asking the house to approve, and far more

effective and compelling reasons must be given before the committee should pass it. I for one intend to support the amendment.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to see hon. members in all parts of the house examine this section. This is an extraordinary power that is being sought. It is over and above anything that has been given before, and I am aware of the amendment that the house passed on another occasion. We are here being asked to give approval to mass snooping into the affairs of Canadians. This is a section that I would have thought the government would have been loath to bring into effect.
In reference to this legislation we have been saying throughout that what is being done is to bring into effect a new principle in connection with old age pension legislation whereby the means test is to be restored. The government endeavours to get around that by explaining that it is not really a means test. They give it another name. This section will make it the meanest test of all. It is an inexcusable intrusion into the rights of the individual. Why should there be one law for the old age pensioner and another law for everybody else? That is what it amounts to. Income tax records of Canadians in general are not looked into except within the limitations of our law. But when it comes to the old age pensioners, that group cannot be trusted. That is what this amounts to. They cannot be trusted. We are going to provide the necessary machinery so they can be hunted down and their representations in connection with their income can be investigated
[DOT] (5:30 p.m.)
The government has even gone so far as to provide a penalty in section 21 for those who commit an offence under section 17. I will read the proposed section 21 to indicate how far it goes. It provides:
Every person who
(a) knowingly makes a false or misleading statement in any application-
This is the law today.
-or statement required or permitted by this act . . . or obtains any benefit payment by false pretences ... or
(d) contravenes section 17, is guilty of an offence punishable on summary conviction.
This is an extraordinary position for a government to take, a government which goes
Old Age Security Act Amendment around the country boasting of what it has done in connection with social security. It makes every old age pensioner who asks for this supplementary payment a person to be suspected, to be snooped upon, to be examined. And if perchance an old age pensioner makes a mistake, he is subject to a penalty as prescribed by this section.
I am amazed to find the government taking this position. They do not need this power. Surely they can rely on the integrity of old age pensioners as much as on the integrity of other Canadians. But the government is going to set them apart and say that when they make statements it will check and cross-check those statements. The government is going to examine the income tax records of the old age pensioners, and if it finds any mistakes the pensioners are going to suffer.
Surely the government is not going to set the old age pensioners apart in a class by themselves to be discriminated against so far as any representations they make as to their income are concerned. If they falsify they deserve to be punished. But the onus of establishing this should be on the Crown. Instead the government puts forward an amendment which in effect casts aspersions on every old age pensioner who makes an application. This amendment puts the government in the position of being able to ferret out, to snoop upon and examine the income tax returns of those who make application for extra assistance.
To me, Mr. Chairman, this is a section that reveals in its nakedness that what this government is doing by this legislation is to bring in the means test, and I repeat that over and over again. I know that the government has denied it but this section reveals what it has in mind. I can just imagine every old age pensioner applying for this additional payment being hunted. All the forces of the law will be after him. The Department of National Revenue will be looking into his records, although he was given to understand when he filed them that they would not be subjected to snooping. When Canadians make income tax returns they make them on the distinct understanding that the information they give will be confidential. That was the basis upon which the law was founded. We are going to remove a basic principle so that the government will be able to do that which they undertook to Canadians would not be done, namely, to regard income tax returns as nonconfidential whenever the government decides it is beneficial so to do.

In other words, they were very solicitous that nothing should be looked into, Mr. Gruber having asked for protection against possible action. What action he had in mind I know not.
I suggest we must have the same solicitude for all Canadians, and I resist, resent and will continue to oppose a measure that is going to place the old age pensioners in Canada in a class of their own.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare; Minister of Amateur Sport
subtopic: PROVISION OF GUARANTEED INCOME SUPPLEMENTS AND DETERMINATION OF PENSIONERS' INCOMES
speechtext: That is not true.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: PROVISION OF GUARANTEED INCOME SUPPLEMENTS AND DETERMINATION OF PENSIONERS' INCOMES
speechtext: The old age pensioner is going to be set apart from the rest of us whose returns cannot be examined. An open season is being declared by this government, through this particular section, against those who make application for the additional $30. The minister laughs at this, but that is what it amounts to. There is to be a closed season for those who are powerful and for the rest of Canadians, but an open season on old age pensioners. I object to that kind of legislation.

speakerposition: Minister of Transport
subtopic: PROVISION OF GUARANTEED INCOME SUPPLEMENTS AND DETERMINATION OF PENSIONERS' INCOMES
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I cannot allow what my hon. friend the Minister of Finance called hypocrisy a little while ago of the gross character to which we have just listened to pass without comment. The right hon. gentleman said that we were making a special class of a certain group of old age pensioners by verifying or seeking means to verify the accuracy of statements they make about their income. Every income taxpayer in this country is subject to the verification of his income tax return by the crown. Surely if the crown is entitled to examine the accuracy of a person's statements when he is obliged to have money taken out of his pocket by the state, the crown is entitled and it is no more humiliating to verify the truth of statements of someone making application to have money put into his pockets by the state.
The right hon. gentleman in his usual, skilful manner confused the facts and the purposes of this legislation by suggesting that a communication from one privy councillor to another, for public purposes only and for the
[Mr. Diefenbaker.)

protection of the revenue, is comparable with the revelation of the private affairs of a taxpayer to some other private person or agent.

subtopic: PROVISION OF GUARANTEED INCOME SUPPLEMENTS AND DETERMINATION OF PENSIONERS' INCOMES
speechtext: The section says officer or employee.

speakerposition: Minister of Transport
subtopic: PROVISION OF GUARANTEED INCOME SUPPLEMENTS AND DETERMINATION OF PENSIONERS' INCOMES
speechtext:
I suggest that this is the grossest possible distortion. If we are going to trust Canadians and are going to say that we will run our affairs simply on the basis of trust, then we will accept everybody's income tax returns and make no verification of them at all. This rule would have to apply to the millionaires to whom the right hon. gentleman referred, the rich and the powerful. We would accept their word. We know that 99 per cent of the taxpayers and 99 per cent of the old age pensioners will submit true returns. We also know that a lot of people may make mistakes.
[DOT] (5:40 p.m.)
It does seem to me that to weep these crocodile tears, and everybody knows that is what they are, is going too far. Nobody can produce them by the gallon as well as the right hon. gentleman, except the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre. I should like to see them in a competition. But the ordinary Canadian will not be fooled by fir's. The ordinary taxpayer paying taxes on $2,000 or $3,000, subject to having the truth of what he says verified by the Minister of National Revenue, will not think there is anything unfair about having verification of a statement of income.

subtopic: PROVISION OF GUARANTEED INCOME SUPPLEMENTS AND DETERMINATION OF PENSIONERS' INCOMES
speechtext: By whom?

speakerposition: Minister of Transport
subtopic: PROVISION OF GUARANTEED INCOME SUPPLEMENTS AND DETERMINATION OF PENSIONERS' INCOMES
speechtext: That verification applies to those who will have some of the tax handed over to them. That is exactly what this process is. We are doing this because people need the money, because we have a social conscience and accept our social responsibilities.

subtopic: PROVISION OF GUARANTEED INCOME SUPPLEMENTS AND DETERMINATION OF PENSIONERS' INCOMES
speechtext:
Where are the crocodile tears
now?

speakerposition: Minister of Transport
subtopic: PROVISION OF GUARANTEED INCOME SUPPLEMENTS AND DETERMINATION OF PENSIONERS' INCOMES
speechtext:
It is only fair to the taxpayers, the small ones as well as the large ones, who contribute to the funds used in this way that we should take reasonable steps to see that what is expended is expended on those for whom parliament intended to have it expended. That is all that is sought to be done in this bill.
The real measure of the hypocrisy of hon. gentlemen opposite is that at 3.30 this afternoon the hon. member for Ontario rose and,
December 16, 1966

speaking for his party, said that his party was satisfied with the rest of the bill. "The government is adamant", he said, "so we are ready to have it passed in half an hour". This present objection was not known by these bright people on the other side, including that distinguished lawyer, the Leader of the Opposition. He did not know anything about this until it was pointed out to him by the N.D.P. That is the measure both of their study of the bill and of their sincerity. It seems to me it is about time we recognized that there is a great difference between a simple verification-

Notwithstanding any other Act or law,
(a) the Minister of National Revenue or any person designated by him for the purpose-
