subtopic: PROVISION OF GUARANTEED INCOME SUPPLEMENTS AND DETERMINATION OF PENSIONERS' INCOMES
speechtext:
Next I want to turn to the Minister of National Health and Welfare and quote some words he spoke on December 5 of this year. He was describing to us that strange, esoteric difference between a needs test and a means test. It is one of those difficult philosophic questions I have found it hard to come to a conclusion upon. The minister made an attempt to describe the means test which, heaven forbid, this government would not think of imposing. But whatever they call it, it is a means test, just that. It involves the examination of the nooks and crannies of a person's financial status, the money he has in the bank, whether he owns a car or a home, the ability of relatives to contribute to his support, his earnings and so on. The government rejects entirely that it is a means test; it is merely applying a needs test. The minister described precisely what this government will not do when he said, as recorded on page 10708 of Hansard for December 5:
No information will be asked for that is not already required for income tax purposes; there will be no snooping, no prying into financial affairs, no demeaning questions. This program is an innovation-
For heavens sake, let us have some honesty from this government. If they consider it necessary to snoop and pry into the affairs of
11278	COMMONS
Old Age Security Act Amendment old age pensioners, let them have the courage to say so instead of pretending as this minister did. The kindest thing I can say about his speech of December 5 is that it was extremely disingenuous. The speech conveyed the impression of the people of Canada that the old people were to be treated as responsible and honest citizens and not as objects of snooping and prying. In the bill we have a clear indication that the government does intend to do all the things the minister described, and the things described are part and parcel of the full means test which he rejected out of hand.
The minister says he is not going to examine the nooks and crannies of a person's financial status, the money he has in the bank, whether he owns a car or home, the ability of relatives to contribute to his support, his earnings and so on. The minister may smile, but the bill reads precisely in these terms. It will bring about the snooping and so on I have described. The investigators can seek any information they want under this section that is received under any other act. In other words, there is no limit to the snooping. I suggest that the minister explain his position again perhaps a little more clearly, a little less disingenuously than he did on December 5.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare; Minister of Amateur Sport
subtopic: PROVISION OF GUARANTEED INCOME SUPPLEMENTS AND DETERMINATION OF PENSIONERS' INCOMES
speechtext:
I want to thank the hon. member for Nanaimo-Cowichan-The Islands. He has been kinder to me than most hon. members. Having been described as Scrooge, mean and miserable I am now described as disingenious. I have improved my standing in the committee. The procedure we propose to follow under the bill has been made clear to the committee. It has been suggested that this is a move without precedent, that we are embarking on a practice which is somehow unCanadian. The hon. member for Peace River, making a point earlier, said he did not like a similar provision in the Canada Pension Plan. The fact is that the law already makes it possible for the Department of National Revenue to exchange information-any information-not with respect to the relatively small number now affected but with respect to five million people.
[DOT] (5:50 p.m.)
The intentions of the government on this point have been made clear from the beginning. We have never concealed from anybody the idea that we would seek information about an individual's income and that we would verify this information with the Department of National Revenue. That has been made clear time and time again, so it ought not to come as any surprise. I do not believe

hon. members can find anything particularly repugnant about this. The hon. member for Wellington South has argued that in order to apply a guaranteed income program it is necessary to know what a person's present income is. We ask pensioners to tell us their income on a simple form which we send to them. They tell us. All that happens here is that the Minister of National Health and Welfare or an officer of the department may ask the Department of National Revenue to verify the information. It may at times be of benefit to pensioners to have this information verified.

subtopic: PROVISION OF GUARANTEED INCOME SUPPLEMENTS AND DETERMINATION OF PENSIONERS' INCOMES
speechtext: Oh, oh.

subtopic: PROVISION OF GUARANTEED INCOME SUPPLEMENTS AND DETERMINATION OF PENSIONERS' INCOMES
speechtext: Oh, oh.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare; Minister of Amateur Sport
subtopic: PROVISION OF GUARANTEED INCOME SUPPLEMENTS AND DETERMINATION OF PENSIONERS' INCOMES

The hon. member for
Winnipeg South Centre said we had nine different ways of checking income.

subtopic: PROVISION OF GUARANTEED INCOME SUPPLEMENTS AND DETERMINATION OF PENSIONERS' INCOMES
speechtext: And I am objecting to every one.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare; Minister of Amateur Sport
subtopic: PROVISION OF GUARANTEED INCOME SUPPLEMENTS AND DETERMINATION OF PENSIONERS' INCOMES
speechtext:
But the hon. member is miscontruing this proposal. The only department to which we can go, at our option, to check this information is the Department of National Revenue. We are coming frankly to parliament and seeking approval to do so in order to administer this program. If we are to make any progress in this country in establishing a guaranteed income program in the future, this seems to be a realistic and sensible authority to seek.
I assure hon. members that it is not the intention to conduct any kind of un-Canadian investigation. This is merely intended as a means of checking the information provided. I am sure that if I came to parliament and put this program before parliament without seeking authority of this kind I would be subjected to great criticism for having failed to make such a provision in the bill.
I have tried to understand the arguments put forward. I think maybe that the developments of the afternoon have led to a certain-high temperature in our proceedings. I hope, nevertheless, that hon. members will realize that this is not an effort to denigrate the standing of old age pensioners but a move to
December 16, 1966

maintain what I consider to be a simple, private method of checking information as necessity arises.

subtopic: PROVISION OF GUARANTEED INCOME SUPPLEMENTS AND DETERMINATION OF PENSIONERS' INCOMES
speechtext:
Having been treated to a tear-jerker by the Minister of Transport, several questions occur to me and I should like to ask the Minister of National Health and Welfare to answer them. The minister told us that because 99 per cent of income tax returns are accurate the same degree of accuracy might be expected in returns from old age pensioners. Why, then, does the hon. gentleman need a staff of 400 persons and 675 employees on a part-time basis to deal with these applications?
Income tax returns are normally sent in during one short season of the year. If only 1 per cent of these returns are likely to be incorrect is it worth engaging 675 employees on a part-time basis to snoop into them and take account of what might be an excess of $5 or $10 beyond what is normally regarded as allowable income? Does the minister really think it is worth the time and the effort to employ 675 people in his department to snoop on a few old age pensioners to make sure they do not get a few extra dollars?

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare; Minister of Amateur Sport
subtopic: PROVISION OF GUARANTEED INCOME SUPPLEMENTS AND DETERMINATION OF PENSIONERS' INCOMES
speechtext: The staff is intended not to snoop on pensioners but to process the hundreds of thousands of applications which will have to be processed. The intention is to recruit a casual staff for a few months in order to get this program into operation.

subtopic: PROVISION OF GUARANTEED INCOME SUPPLEMENTS AND DETERMINATION OF PENSIONERS' INCOMES
speechtext:

need for extra staff only arises at certain times of the year. How does he explain that?

subtopic: PROVISION OF GUARANTEED INCOME SUPPLEMENTS AND DETERMINATION OF PENSIONERS' INCOMES

One of the claims the minister keeps making is that the test of income embodied in this legislation is not the kind of means test which has been incorporated in the past in other legislation. I draw his attention to the fact that in the original Old Age Pensions Act, which did contain a means test -there is no doubt about that-no provision was made for getting information from the income tax branch. I also draw the hon. gentleman's attention to the fact that at the present time there is a means test embodied in the War Veterans Allowance Act. Yet I know of no provision in that act which enables the government to get information from the Department of National Revenue with respect to veterans who apply for allowances.
Business of the House
I submit that the government is writing into this legislation a method of checking which has not been used in relation to other means tests. This places the minister in a difficult position when he maintains he is offering a pension which people get after filling out a simple form, being trusted all the time. I believe the minister should think about this over the week end, since it is now six o'clock.
